name: Syphilis (VDRL/RPR)
summary: VDRL and RPR are non-treponemal blood tests used to screen for syphilis (infection with the bacterium Treponema pallidum). They detect reagin antibodies the immune system makes against fat-like (cardiolipin) material released from cells damaged during infection, rather than antibodies against the bacterium itself.
whatItMeans: A non-reactive result means no reagin antibodies were detected and syphilis is unlikely, though very early (primary) or very late infection can still read non-reactive, so timing and exposure history matter. A reactive result is only a screen and is not a diagnosis: it must be confirmed with a treponemal test (such as FTA-ABS or TPPA), because non-treponemal tests can produce biological false positives from pregnancy, autoimmune disease, or other infections. When infection is confirmed, the test is repeated as a numeric titer (for example 1:8 or 1:32); a fourfold drop in titer generally indicates a good response to treatment, while a fourfold rise can signal reinfection or treatment failure. This is educational information, not a diagnosis, and results should always be interpreted by a clinician.
confounders: Biological false positives (pregnancy, autoimmune disease such as lupus or antiphospholipid syndrome, other infections, IV drug use, older age, recent vaccination)
Prozone effect: very high antibody titers can cause a falsely non-reactive or weakly reactive result unless the sample is diluted
Window period: early primary or late latent syphilis may read non-reactive despite infection
A treponemal confirmatory test is required before interpreting a reactive screen; VDRL and RPR titers are not interchangeable and should be trended on the same test
Assay method and each laboratory's cutoffs vary, so results and titers can differ between labs
